solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Some neck on this gaffer, screwing around Cyclops!

indicators.note: screwing is twisting, so the letters are wrung into a different order
to go around something is to enclose it, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: the word taken as written, ready to be twisted
the setter, Cyclops, refers to himself as I

explanation.surface: A cheeky boss with plenty of neck is messing about with the setter.
explanation.walkthrough: Neck here is cheek, as in nerve, on the surface; the definition takes it literally as the long body part. Cyclops is the setter's name, and setters refer to themselves as I or ME.
explanation.definitionFit: The animal with the longest neck of any creature is the obvious thing to have some neck, read literally.

clue.text: Elected, yet Boris perversely exhibits a tosspot quality

indicators.note: acting perversely means going the wrong way, so the letters come out in a wrong order

blocks.note: a candidate who is elected is in
both words taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson wins an election yet still behaves like a drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: A tosspot is an old word for a heavy drinker, so the quality is drunkenness.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of sobriety, meaning habitual drunkenness, is exactly the characteristic of a heavy drinker.

clue.text: Musicians' testes crushed no end, with unknown insert

definitions.note: the possessive reads as plural musicians; the answer is a noun for a group of them

indicators.note: with no end, the final letter is cut away
something crushed is mashed out of shape, so the letters are jumbled
an insert is put inside something else, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: the word with its last letter removed
in algebra an unknown is x

explanation.surface: A crude picture of musicians' private parts being squashed.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive on the definition is a nudge: the answer is the group the musicians form.
explanation.definitionFit: Six performers playing together are called by this word, so it names a group of musicians.

clue.text: Dump thousands of dollars in sorrow

indicators.note: one thing placed in another is enclosed by it

blocks.note: pity is sorrow felt for another
a grand, G, is a thousand dollars, so several are Gs

explanation.surface: Someone sadly throws away a fortune.
explanation.walkthrough: Dump reads as a verb, to throw away, but it is the noun for a filthy place. G for grand is slang for a thousand.
explanation.definitionFit: A pigsty is figuratively any squalid, messy room, which is what calling a place a dump means.

clue.text: see 21ac.
(*11ac./25dn.) Contrary saboteur getting pissed in a squalid cafe

indicators.note: someone getting drunk loses order, so these letters stagger into a new arrangement
squalid means sordid and messed up, so these letters are disordered too
to be in something is to be enclosed by it

blocks.note: taken as written
the word taken as written, to be rearranged
the word taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: An awkward wrecker gets drunk in a grubby greasy spoon.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumbled saboteur sits between A and the jumbled cafe. Arse about face is British slang for back to front or the wrong way round.
explanation.definitionFit: The slang phrase means the wrong way round, and contrary can mean opposite in direction or order.

clue.text: Ken, right tit mangled – "a mere trifle"

indicators.note: something mangled is crushed out of shape, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the usual abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone tells Ken that a mangled nipple, or bird, is nothing much.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make the definition look like Ken's reported speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A trinket is a small ornament of little value, which is a synonym for a trifle.

clue.text: Elected, miss being poor?

blocks.note: an elected candidate is in
to miss something is to want or need it

explanation.surface: A newly elected politician wonders whether missing out means poverty.
explanation.walkthrough: Miss looks like a young woman, or a failure to hit, but it is the verb meaning to lack.
explanation.definitionFit: People in need lack money or necessities, which is the state of being poor.

clue.text: Nick on Brenda's 'crook'

indicators.note: one thing set on another is placed next to it, here ahead of it

blocks.note: to nick is to steal, to pilfer
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, whose cipher is ER

explanation.surface: Someone called Nick works for the Queen as her shepherd's crook, or her criminal.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye has long called Queen Elizabeth II Brenda; ER is her royal cipher. Nick reads as a man's name but is the verb to steal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilferer steals small things, and a crook is any criminal or thief.

clue.text: Undermine politician after one broadcast

indicators.note: one thing coming after another is placed behind it in the sequence

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
Member of Parliament
to broadcast is to air

explanation.surface: A politician undermines a rival after one programme goes out.
explanation.walkthrough: Broadcast looks like a verb in the surface sense of a show going out; it supplies a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To impair something is to weaken or damage it, which is the sense of undermine.

clue.text: see 6dn.
Following May's lead, Gove is adapting force, as bad leaders do

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for the verb

indicators.note: the lead of something is its front, so only the initial letter is kept
adapting means altering to fit, so the letters are refashioned
what follows comes behind, setting the order of the pieces

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name
both words taken as written, to be rearranged
the Royal Navy, RN, is an armed force

explanation.surface: Michael Gove follows Theresa May's example and uses force, as poor leaders do.
explanation.walkthrough: Theresa May and Michael Gove were senior Conservative politicians; May was Prime Minister. The definition is a whole phrase describing what the answer does.
explanation.definitionFit: To misgovern is to rule a country badly, which is what incompetent heads of state do.

clue.text: At the outset, roping in a Democrat as a questionable Trump supporter

indicators.note: to be in something is to be enclosed, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: at the outset means first
to lay a rope is to twist its strands together
D is the abbreviation for a Democrat

explanation.surface: A campaign lassoes a Democrat early on, presenting them as a dubious backer of Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: The wife of a US president is called the First Lady; questionable hints at Melania Trump's doubtful enthusiasm for her husband.
explanation.definitionFit: Melania Trump, as the president's wife, is expected to stand behind him, so she is his official spouse and backer.

clue.text: Pick-up ruse?

blocks.note: first meaning: an American make of pick-up truck
second meaning: a trick or evasive scheme

explanation.walkthrough: Pick-up ruse sounds like a chat-up line; the two words are separate meanings. Dodge is an American motor brand known for its Ram pick-up trucks.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both a vehicle maker whose trucks are pick-ups and a noun for a cunning trick.

clue.text: Dim Capitol's reinvented 'opposite of Trump'?

indicators.note: something reinvented is made over in a new form, so these letters are rebuilt

blocks.note: both words taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A dull Washington is remade as the antithesis of Donald Trump.
explanation.walkthrough: The Capitol is the US Congress building in Washington; the apostrophe s is 'is', joining wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tactful and careful in dealings is the reverse of Trump's famously blunt, undiplomatic style.

clue.text: In Boris's eyes, doing a U-turn is an emphatic assertion

indicators.note: what is in a phrase sits within its letters
a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the letters sit across the end of the name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson thinks a policy reversal is a firm statement.
explanation.walkthrough: The run of letters spans the two words and reads right to left. Boris Johnson was notorious for U-turns.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an emphatic way of saying yes, an exclamation of strong agreement or affirmation.

clue.text: Hit with Trump's openers, revolt on the outside

indicators.note: openers come at the start, so the leading letters are taken
being on the outside means wrapping round, so one piece encloses the other

blocks.note: the opening pair of letters of the name
to revolt is to disgust, to sicken

explanation.surface: Something hit hard by Trump's first moves, with a rebellion all around.
explanation.walkthrough: Revolt looks like a noun for an uprising, but it is the verb meaning to disgust.
explanation.definitionFit: Stricken is an old past participle of strike, so it means hit or struck, often by illness or misfortune.

clue.text: Parrot swallows article cover

indicators.note: what swallows something takes it inside

blocks.note: to parrot is to copy
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: A pet bird eats a magazine piece's cover.
explanation.walkthrough: Parrot reads as the bird doing the swallowing, but it is the verb meaning to imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: A canopy is an overhead covering such as a cloth awning, so it is a kind of cover.

clue.text: Pickled like a herring?

blocks.note: first meaning: drunk, in British slang
second meaning: sealed in a tin, as fish often are

explanation.walkthrough: Pickled herring is a real dish, so the clue reads as one idea; pickled is in fact slang for drunk, a separate meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is British slang for drunk and also describes food preserved in a tin.

clue.text: Cyclops upset May with alternative role for press

indicators.note: something upset is knocked over and disordered
an alternative form is a different arrangement of the same thing

blocks.note: the setter, Cyclops, refers to himself as I
Theresa May is an MP, a Member of Parliament
taken as written

explanation.surface: The setter annoys Theresa May by offering the media a different job.
explanation.walkthrough: May is the politician Theresa May, standing for MP. Press looks like the media, but it is the verb meaning to urge.
explanation.definitionFit: To implore someone is to beg or urge them earnestly, which is to press them.

clue.text: Maybe hardline Corbynites feel it's wrong

indicators.note: wrong means not in proper order, so the letters are out of place

blocks.note: the words taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Perhaps hard-left Corbyn supporters think something is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: Jeremy Corbyn was a left-wing Labour leader; Maybe marks his followers as an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Supporters of a socialist Labour leader are left-wingers, called by the informal plural noun.

clue.text: (& 5dn.) No favourite of Trump, normal food, NY variety, with zero filling

indicators.note: a variety is a different version, so these letters are reordered
a filling sits inside something else, so one piece is put within another

blocks.note: the words taken as written, to be rearranged
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: Trump dislikes ordinary New York-style food stuffed with nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: The holder of this office, Sadiq Khan, had a long public feud with Donald Trump.
explanation.definitionFit: Sadiq Khan, the elected head of the British capital, was repeatedly insulted by Trump, so hardly his friend.

clue.text: Tabloid hits Pat with "PHEW WHAT A SCORCHER!" consequence?

blocks.note: The Sun is a British tabloid newspaper
a pat is a gentle stroke

explanation.surface: A tabloid lands a story on someone called Pat with a heatwave headline.
explanation.walkthrough: PHEW WHAT A SCORCHER! is the stock Sun headline for a hot day. Pat reads as a name, but it is a light touch.
explanation.definitionFit: Illness from too much hot weather is a natural result of the heatwave that headline celebrates.

clue.text: A short time back

blocks.note: first meaning: a brief moment
to support a proposal

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a time not long ago; back is really the verb meaning to support.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a brief unit of time and also a verb for formally supporting a motion.

clue.text: Old boy besieged by knockers – very much

indicators.note: a place besieged is surrounded on all sides

blocks.note: both are slang for breasts
OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: An old man surrounded by critics, or by breasts, enjoys it greatly.
explanation.walkthrough: Knockers could be critics, but here it is slang for breasts. The phrase is used in British speech as in loving someone to bits.
explanation.definitionFit: Loving someone to bits means loving them enormously, so the idiom is an intensifier.

clue.text: Cradle-to-grave biography: 'Boris's London Transport'

definitions.note: an adjective phrase standing for the noun

blocks.note: a biography is a life of someone
Boris bikes are London's public hire bicycles, introduced while Johnson was mayor

explanation.surface: A full biography of Boris Johnson titled after his London transport scheme.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris bikes, named after Boris Johnson, are the hire bicycles of London's public cycle scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: The full course from birth to death is what cradle-to-grave describes, the whole span of a living thing.

clue.text: see 6dn.
Frantic party puts one right off ex-PM by the way

indicators.note: putting something off removes it, so letters are taken away

blocks.note: I is one and R is right, the letters to remove
Tony Blair is a former Prime Minister
ST, street, is a way

explanation.surface: A wild party at which a former Prime Minister makes one change his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove I and R from the former Prime Minister, then add the street abbreviation. By the way reads as an aside, but it marks placing beside a way.
explanation.definitionFit: A blast is informal for a riotously good time, the sort of wild, hectic party described.

clue.text: Coward wrecking career with conservative body

indicators.note: something wrecked is smashed up, so its letters are scattered

blocks.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
the National Trust, NT, is a British heritage conservation charity

explanation.surface: A cowardly politician ruins his career by joining a Tory group.
explanation.walkthrough: Conservative here is small c: the body conserves buildings and land, not the Tory party.
explanation.definitionFit: Recreant is an archaic, literary word for a cowardly or craven person who yields.

clue.text: Habit attributed to Trump sources: wrath!

indicators.note: a source is where something begins, so the initial letters are taken

blocks.note: the opening letters of the three words
ire is anger, wrath

explanation.surface: A habit of anger is ascribed to Trump by insiders.
explanation.walkthrough: Habit reads as a tendency, as in an angry streak, but it is clothing, as a nun's habit.
explanation.definitionFit: A habit is a distinctive garment, and attire is clothing, so both name what is worn.
